MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge
To support independent evaluation while preventing benchmark contamination, MKA is accompanied by two disjoint task sets.
MKA (200 tasks) is the private evaluation suite reported in this paper, hosted and graded independently on a public leaderboard by Artificial Analysis using the open-source Stirrup framework
MKA-Showcase (10 tasks) is a separate, publicly downloadable release of one task per sector with full prompts, input files, and grading rubrics.
MKA consists of 200 real-world tasks written and verified by vetted domain professionals.

The tasks are split evenly across 10 sectors (20 tasks each) and cover 83 occupations, including financial analysts, licensed architects, electrical and mechanical engineers, GIS surveyors, data scientists, attorneys and physicians.
Each author has at least five years of professional experience, and every task was reviewed for realism and accuracy by a second expert with the same job profile.

An expert spent 3 to 8 hours on each task: assembling a realistic multi-file input bundle, solving the task to produce golden reference deliverables, and writing a grading rubric with a golden justification for every criterion.
Figure 1 illustrates how the 200 tasks are distributed evenly across 10 sectors (20 tasks, or 10.0%, per sector) and 83 occupations.
Business: management consultants, marketing and media analysts, customer support specialists, revenue management analysts and procurement specialists.
Construction: licensed architects, construction estimators, quantity surveyors, real estate appraisers and civil or fire protection engineers.
Education: K–12 and university instructors, curriculum compliance analysts, academic moderators, school psychologists and training specialists.
Engineering: mechanical and CAD engineers, electrical and RF engineers, chemical process engineers, power systems engineers and manufacturing quality engineers.
Finance: financial and investment analysts, accountants and auditors, property and marine underwriters, credit analysts and tax preparers.
Healthcare: diagnostic and pediatric radiologists, radiation oncologists, telestroke neurologists, hospital administrators and medical coding or claims specialists.
Law and government: immigration, corporate, real estate and patent attorneys, regulatory analysts, municipal procurement officers and government administrators.
Logistics and mapping: GIS analysts, land surveyors, urban and regional transport planners, precision agriculture analysts and logistics analysts.
Science: clinical trial researchers, medicinal and analytical chemists, molecular and wildlife biologists, materials scientists and EEG analysts.
Software and data: front-end engineers, data analysts, data engineers, software QA engineers and radio or network engineers.
Each task includes 2 to 45 input files (1,459 in total; mean 7.30, median 6.0), and solving it requires combining information across visual, tabular, document and geospatial formats.

harder frontier suites such as MMMU (Yue et al., 2024a), CharXiv (Wang et al., 2024c), and MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2024b) require strong visual perception, but present pre-selected images or pages in a single, tool-free turn and grade multiple-choice or short text answers.

GUI and Computer-Use Environments. Browser and desktop benchmarks (Li et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2024) evaluate agents acting through low-level pixel coordinates (mouse_move, click(x, y)) or DOM actions
APEX-Agents (Vidgen et al., 2026) places agents in multi-file worlds across banking, consulting, and law, grading outputs via per-criterion LLM-judge calls (Pass@1).
GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2025) spans 44 occupations and grades deliverables primarily via blinded pairwise preference.
deep-research benchmarks evaluate multi-step web search over text (BrowseComp; Wei et al. 2025) and visual web content (MM-BrowseComp; Li et al. 2025b).

Surge AI’s GDP.pdf (Garre et al., 2026) evaluates atomic criterion rubrics over dense, multi-document professional PDFs, yet still pre-attaches source PDFs in a single-turn prompt and grades a text response via a text-only judge
We evaluate every model in Stirrup (v0.2.1) (Artificial Analysis, 2025), an open-source, lightweight agent framework maintained by Artificial Analysis.
All models use the same harness, system instructions, tool set, container image and resource budgets; only the model endpoint changes.
Stirrup runs without human intervention until the agent calls finish or reaches the limit of 250 turns, with up to a 1M-token context window if available, and an 8-hour wall-clock limit per task.
At 70% of the model’s context length, compaction is triggered.
In the final 20 turns, the harness appends a warning with the number of remaining turns so the agent can finish and submit its deliverables.
Each task runs in a fresh, isolated Linux container (4 vCPUs; 128 MB base RAM dynamically bursting up to 16 GB) based on a Debian container with Python 3.13
The sandbox has internet access.
The image includes common document, PDF, OCR and rendering tools, including LibreOffice, Tesseract, pymupdf, weasyprint and Python Office libraries
Stirrup exposes four tools: code_exec, view_image, web_search and finish.
code_exec runs bash commands and Python scripts (300 s per-command timeout), and web_search issues web queries (180 s timeout).
view_image loads a raster image (.png, .jpg, .webp, .gif, .bmp or .tiff) into the model’s visual context.
view_image is designed to respect the native image resolution of the output file.
At the end of a trajectory, finish checks that every declared deliverable exists and ends the session.
The Agentic Autorater is also a Stirrup agent.
It runs in its own fresh container with code_exec, view_image and a structured submit_verdicts finish tool, and without web access.
The autorater does not receive the task’s input files: MKA rubrics are self-contained, with each criterion stating the expected value, tolerance or property directly
We use OpenAI GPT-6 Luna as the autorater model.

Treating the human majority verdict as ground truth yields an autorater error rate of 3.8% [2.4, 5.4] per criterion (about one error in 26 criteria).

False passes mainly reflect boundary leniency, such as crediting alternative or non-primary values when the model’s committed answer differs, or accepting semantically equivalent content when a required label is omitted.
Task WSR is the weighted share of satisfied criteria
All metrics are task-level means with tasks weighted equally.

Using a fixed panel of four prior-generation models (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol), we label a criterion regression if every model in the panel passes it in at least 2 of 3 runs (6,396 criteria across 180 tasks), and climb otherwise (7,888 criteria across all 200 tasks).

Because this split is derived from autorater verdicts, a small fraction of criteria the panel satisfies may also be labeled climb due to judge false fails (Section 3.3); the 2-of-3 rule dampens single-run flips, and the frozen split applies equally to all evaluated models.

Climb-WSR (headline; frontier capability), Regression-WSR (retention of skills that prior-generation models already have, averaged over the 180 tasks with regression criteria) and Overall WSR (overall deliverable quality).
All four models saturate Regression-WSR above 95% (95.17%–96.36%), confirming that frontier differences are concentrated in Climb-WSR.

the top three models—Claude Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Carbon, and Claude Opus 5.5 (53.01% Climb-WSR, 70.98% Overall WSR)—are statistically indistinguishable on Climb-WSR (Fable 5.2 vs. Carbon: +2.22 pp, 95% CI [−0.94, +5.49]; Carbon vs. Opus 5.5: +1.33 pp, 95% CI [−1.70, +4.41])
both Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon significantly outperform GPT-6 Astra (50.24% Climb-WSR, 69.34% Overall WSR; Carbon vs. Astra: +4.10 pp Climb-WSR, 95% CI [+1.00, +7.11])
Even for the strongest frontier models, Climb-WSR remains around 54%–57%, leaving substantial headroom to evaluate multimodal agent progress.

Most knowledge work benchmarks can be solved with text alone, without ever needing to look at an image or page layout.
We built MKA to measure how well agents can handle this visually complex work.
we partnered with domain experts across 10 verticals and 83 occupations where day-to-day work is inherently visual
created MKA's 200-task evaluation set to assist them in their jobs
The Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, developed with Artificial Analysis, evaluates how agents reason across visually complex files to solve real-world knowledge work tasks.
